goals.title: U0 · Vector arithmetic refresher
goals.description: Use plane and space coordinates, linear combinations and dot products in preparation for linear systems.

goals.title: Start the vector refresher
goals.description: The learner can say which vector skills the refresher will check. Read and write ordered components, find the displacement between two points, combine vectors and take a dot product. The short check uses both a pair and a triple.

goals.title: Read and write vector components
goals.description:
The learner can read and write ordered vector components in the plane and in space. Fix the order of the axes. For a vector drawn from the origin, read its signed changes along x and y, and along z in space. For example, two units left and three up have components (−2, 3). The spatial vector (1, −2, 4) has x-component 1, y-component −2 and z-component 4.

At 10:42 and 23:12 in Lecture 1, read the components of the planar and spatial arrows on the board.

goals.title: Compute a displacement from two points
goals.description: The learner can compute the displacement vector from a start point to an end point. Use the same coordinate order for both points. Subtract the start coordinate from the end coordinate in each position. From (2, −1, 0) to (3, 1, −2), the displacement is (3 − 2, 1 − (−1), −2 − 0) = (1, 2, −2).

goals.title: Compute a linear combination
goals.description:
The learner can compute a given linear combination of vectors. Multiply each vector by its scalar, then add component by component. For example, 2(1, 2) + (0, 1) = (2, 5).

At 12:16 in Lecture 1, follow the two scaled columns and their geometric sum. Then compute the different combination given here.

goals.title: Compute a dot product
goals.description:
The learner can compute the dot product of two vectors with the same number of components. Multiply entries in corresponding positions and add the products to get a number. For example, (2, −1) · (3, 4) = 6 − 4 = 2.

At 4:20 in Lecture 14, identify the corresponding entries in the symbolic dot-product formula. Then try the numerical example above.

goals.title: Check your vector arithmetic
goals.description: Use ordered components, displacement, a linear combination and a dot product.

examData.taskContent:
1. An arrow starts at the origin of a plane and goes 2 units in the negative x direction and 3 units in the positive y direction. Give its ordered vector components. Then give the displacement from (1, −2, 4) to (3, −1, 2).
2. With p = (1, −1, 2) and q = (3, 0, 1), calculate 2p − q. Show the scaled vector and componentwise subtraction.
3. Calculate p · q and show the products you add.

steps.description: Give the vector components (−2, 3) in x, y order.
Give the displacement (2, 1, −2) from start to end.
Scale p to (2, −2, 4).
Subtract q component by component from the learner’s stated 2p. Award this point if that subtraction is correct. A scaling slip is charged only at the scaling step.
Pair the corresponding entries in the dot product.
Sum the products the learner showed. Award this point for a correct sum even if a product was wrong at the previous step.

goals.title: Start linear systems
goals.description:
The learner can state the unit plan and the success criteria. First read a system as an intersection and as a weighted sum of columns, and write its matrix form. Then solve by elimination and back substitution and classify the solutions. The two closing tasks check those skills in that order. MIT lectures write Ax = b. Here we write Au = b because x, y and z name individual unknowns and u names the vector that contains them.

At 1:21 in Lecture 1, listen for the introduction of the two pictures and matrix notation, then name the steps you will use here.

goals.title: Interpret the row picture
goals.description:
The learner can interpret a solution set as the common intersection of lines or planes. A nonzero coefficient row describes a line in two unknowns or a plane in three. A solution lies on every one of these sets. In the figure, x + y = 3 and x + 2y = 5 define two lines that meet at (1, 2). To test a proposed point, substitute its coordinates in each equation.

In Lecture 1, compare the two-line example at 4:20 with the planes drawn from 17:31. In each, identify what the geometric objects have in common.

goals.title: Write a system as Au = b
goals.description:
The learner can encode a linear system as Au = b with a fixed variable order. A matrix is a rectangular array with entries arranged in rows and columns. Put the coefficient of each variable in the corresponding column of its equation’s row. Write a zero for an absent variable. Put the unknowns into u in variable order and put the right-hand sides into b in equation order. Both are column vectors.

```text
⎡x⎤
⎢y⎥  =  (x, y, z)ᵀ
⎣z⎦
```

The superscript ᵀ turns the horizontal tuple into the displayed column. For 2x − z = 4 with u in the order x, y, z, the coefficient row is (2, 0, −1) and its entry in b is 4.

At 2:27 in Lecture 1, trace the coefficients of each equation into its matrix row. Look for the order in which the entries are written.

goals.title: Interpret the column picture
goals.description:
The learner can explain how a solution vector gives the weights in a column combination. The entries of a solution vector are weights whose weighted column sum equals b. In the figure the two columns are (1, 1)ᵀ and (1, 2)ᵀ. The weights 1 and 2 give 1(1, 1)ᵀ + 2(1, 2)ᵀ = (3, 5)ᵀ. The column picture uses right-hand-side coordinates b₁ and b₂. The row picture uses the unknowns x and y.

At 8:47 and 22:04 in Lecture 1, trace the weights in the two-column and three-column examples. Find the target vector each sum has to produce.

goals.title: Multiply a matrix by a vector
goals.description:
The learner can compute Av by a weighted column sum and by row dot products. For an m × n matrix A, v has n components and Av has m. To compute by columns, multiply each column by its corresponding component of v and add the results. To compute by rows, take each row’s dot product with v and collect the results in row order. If A has rows (2, 1) and (0, 3) and v = (1, −1)ᵀ, both methods give (1, −3)ᵀ.

At 36:01 in Lecture 1, follow both ways of computing the same product on the board. Check that they list the result entries in the same order.

goals.title: Eliminate to triangular form
goals.description:
The learner can reduce a square system by equivalent row operations to upper triangular form, showing pivots, multipliers and row exchanges. Upper triangular means all entries below the main diagonal are zero. Append b to A and apply each operation to the entire row so the equations keep the same solutions.

The symbol aᵢⱼ denotes the entry in row i and column j of the current coefficient matrix. At each step look for a nonzero entry in the active column at or below the active row. The chosen nonzero entry of the current matrix is the pivot. If it is below the active row, swap the rows to bring it up. If there is no candidate, go to the next column without advancing the active row.

If aₖⱼ is the pivot in row k, clear aᵢⱼ below it with Rᵢ ← Rᵢ − (aᵢⱼ/aₖⱼ)Rₖ. Then move down a row and right a column. For x + 2y = 4 and 3x + 7y = 13, the multiplier 3 leaves y = 1 in the second row.

At 2:34 in Lecture 2, trace the column-clearing steps and the final pivots. At 11:02, look for the coefficient change that makes a swap necessary. At 14:52, follow the same operations on the added right-hand-side column.

goals.title: Solve by back substitution
goals.description:
The learner can solve an upper triangular system with nonzero diagonal entries by back substitution. An upper triangular coefficient matrix has zeros below its main diagonal. The bottom equation determines the last unknown. Work upward, substituting the values already known and isolating the remaining unknown in each row. For x + y = 5, y − z = 1 and 2z = 6, work upwards to get z = 3, y = 4 and x = 1.

At 17:11 in Lecture 2, follow the board solution from the lowest equation upward. Record which unknown is found at each step.

goals.title: Classify the solutions of a linear system
goals.description:
The learner can decide whether a square system has exactly one, infinitely many, or no solutions over the real numbers and explain the result in both pictures. A square coefficient matrix is singular if elimination finishes with fewer pivots than unknowns. A row exchange can fix one candidate even for a matrix that turns out to be singular.

A contradictory row such as 0 = 1 rules out a common intersection. With a pivot in every variable column, back substitution fixes each unknown, so the row picture has one point and the column picture has one choice of weights. With a missing pivot and no contradiction, at least one variable is free. Its value can vary over the reals, and solving for the pivot variables gives infinitely many solutions.

The span of the columns is the set of all their weighted sums. A system is consistent exactly when b lies in the span. Every right-hand side is attainable exactly when the columns span the entire right-hand-side space.

For x + y = 1 and 2x + 2y = t, the columns are both (1, 2)ᵀ. If t = 2, the lines coincide and b lies in the span. Both (1, 0) and (0, 1) solve the equations because either weight choice gives (1, 2)ᵀ. If t differs from 2, the lines do not meet and b lies outside the span.

At 31:06 in Lecture 1, compare attainable right-hand sides for related columns. At 5:31 and 12:10 in Lecture 8, interpret the zero-row condition and the choices left by a free variable.

goals.title: Recall linear systems
goals.description: Retrieve the meanings and short rules used in the column picture, matrix-vector multiplication, elimination, back substitution and consistency.

goals.title: Closing task 1 · The two pictures and matrix form
goals.description: Interpret two systems, encode one as Au = b, describe its column picture and compute a matrix–vector product in both ways. The pass mark is 13 of 16.

examData.taskContent:
1. For x + y = 4 and x + 2y = 5, name the objects in the row picture. Find their common point and show why it lies on both.

2. Use the system

   x + y = 3
   2x + 2y + z = 7
   x + 2y + z = 6

   Name the objects in its row picture. Check whether (1, 2, 1) lies on all of them.

3. Write the three-variable system as Au = b in the order x, y, z. Give the columns of A and write their weighted-sum equation. Explain what a solution vector gives you in the column picture. Say which quantities the coordinates describe in each picture.

4. For v = (2, 1, 0)ᵀ, compute Av by row dot products and independently by a weighted sum of the columns. Show both setups and their results.

Show your work. Method points follow through from the earlier values you show, and a single arithmetic slip is charged once.
examData.solutionContent:
1. The equations describe two lines. Subtracting the first equation from the second gives y = 1, so x = 3. The checks are 3 + 1 = 4 and 3 + 2 = 5, so (3, 1) lies on both.

2. The three equations describe planes. Substituting (1, 2, 1) gives 1 + 2 = 3, 2 + 4 + 1 = 7, and 1 + 4 + 1 = 6. The point lies on all three planes.

3. A has rows (1, 1, 0), (2, 2, 1), and (1, 2, 1). The unknown column is u = (x, y, z)ᵀ and b = (3, 7, 6)ᵀ. The columns of A are c₁ = (1, 2, 1)ᵀ, c₂ = (1, 2, 2)ᵀ, and c₃ = (0, 1, 1)ᵀ. The column equation is xc₁ + yc₂ + zc₃ = b. A solution gives weights whose weighted sum reaches b. In the row picture, coordinates are values of the unknowns. In the column picture, coordinates are right-hand-side entries.

4. The row dot products with v give 2 + 1 + 0, 4 + 2 + 0, and 2 + 2 + 0 in row order. This gives (3, 6, 4)ᵀ. By columns, 2c₁ + c₂ + 0c₃ = (2, 4, 2)ᵀ + (1, 2, 2)ᵀ = (3, 6, 4)ᵀ.

steps.description: Identify the two lines.
Find (3, 1) and justify that it satisfies both equations.
Identify the three planes.
Check the three equations at (1, 2, 1) and interpret the point as belonging to all three planes.
Record the coefficient of each variable, including the zero for the absent z term.
Arrange the learner’s stated coefficient triples as rows in equation order. Award the method point even if an individual coefficient was wrong.
Write the column vector u in the order x, y, z. Accept a vertical column or an explicitly stated column convention.
Put (3, 7, 6) into a right-hand-side column in equation order.
Read the three columns from the learner’s displayed A in the correct order.
Use the entries x, y and z as weights in the same order as the learner’s displayed columns.
Show that the weighted sum must equal the right-hand-side vector b.
Distinguish right-hand-side coordinates in the column picture from unknown coordinates in the row picture.
Set up the dot product with v for each displayed row of A and keep the row order.
Set up the sum of the learner’s displayed columns weighted by 2, 1 and 0 respectively. A term with coefficient zero may be omitted.
Evaluate the displayed row dot products and present the ordered result. Award for correct evaluation using the learner’s earlier coefficients.
Evaluate the displayed weighted column sum. Follow through from earlier coefficients or intermediate values. Count an arithmetic slip again only if it is independent of a slip already charged.

goals.title: Closing task 2 · Elimination and what it reveals
goals.description: Eliminate, solve by back substitution and classify related real systems in both pictures. The pass mark is 12 of 15.

examData.taskContent:
1. Solve the system

   x + y = 3
   2x + 2y + z = 7
   x + 2y + z = 6

   Keep the first equation as your first pivot row and use it to clear the first column below it. Show your multipliers and the operations on the entire equations. Show how you deal with the next zero pivot candidate. Label your pivots, write the upper triangular system and solve it by back substitution. Explain why there is exactly one solution in both pictures.

2. Replace only the third equation by x + y + z = s. After clearing the first column as before, can a row exchange provide a y-pivot? Eliminate further and give the final equation. For s = 4 and for s = 5, say how many real solutions exist and explain why in both pictures. When there are infinitely many, give two different solutions as witnesses.

Show your work. Valid methods are scored against the equations you display. Correct follow-through earns method points and a single arithmetic slip is charged once.
examData.solutionContent:
1. Keep the first equation as the initial pivot row. Subtract 2R₁ from R₂ to obtain z = 1. Subtract R₁ from R₃ to obtain y + z = 3. The multipliers are 2 and 1. Swap the two lower rows to move the nonzero y-entry into the second row. The upper triangular equations are x + y = 3, y + z = 3, and z = 1, with pivots 1, 1 and 1 in order.

   Read z = 1 from the bottom. In the middle row substitute z to obtain y = 3 − 1 = 2. In the top row substitute y to obtain x = 3 − 2 = 1. Each variable is determined, so (1, 2, 1) is the only common point of the three planes. It is also the only choice of column weights that reaches b, because any other such choice would solve the same equations.

2. After the same first-column eliminations the lower equations are z = 1 and z = s − 3. Both remaining y entries are zero. A swap between the lower rows cannot provide a y-pivot. Use the z-pivot and subtract the second row from the third to obtain 0 = s − 4.

   For s = 4 the three planes share the line specified by x + y = 3 and z = 1. The last row is 0 = 0, so there are infinitely many real solutions. Two examples are (0, 3, 1) and (3, 0, 1). In the column picture c₁ = c₂ = (1, 2, 1)ᵀ and c₃ = (0, 1, 1)ᵀ. The vector b = (3, 7, 4)ᵀ equals 3c₁ + c₃. The total weight 3 on the identical first two columns can be shared in infinitely many ways.

   For s = 5 the third plane misses the line of the first two planes. Its equation would require x + y + z = 5 along a line on which that sum is 4. There is no solution. In the column picture the first two coordinates of b force x + y = 3 and z = 1. The third coordinate of the weighted sum is therefore 4. The requested b = (3, 7, 5)ᵀ lies outside the span.

steps.description: Show reversible operations for clearing below the first pivot and apply them to the augmented equations. Award the method point for correct use of the stated multipliers even if a multiplier computation was wrong.
Calculate the multipliers appropriate to the displayed current pivot and entries. On the requested path these are 2 and 1.

Handle the next pivot correctly for the displayed equivalent system. The requested path detects the zero candidate and swaps with a row carrying a nonzero y-entry. For a valid alternative path, accept a justified nonzero pivot from that path.
Display an upper triangular system following from the shown operations. Accept valid equivalent paths and correct continuation using earlier values.
Label the selected nonzero entries as pivots for the learner’s path. On the requested path they are 1, 1 and 1 in order.
Start from the bottom equation of the displayed upper triangular system and isolate its last unknown.
Use the learner’s own value of the last unknown in the middle equation and isolate the middle unknown.
Use the learner’s own earlier values in the first equation as needed and isolate the first unknown.
Evaluate the isolated expressions accurately using the learner’s values from earlier steps. Charge an arithmetic slip only where it originates.
Report the values reached by back substitution in the stated variable order, following through from the learner’s results.
Explain that the nonzero pivots fix the unknowns and that the ordinary system has both one common point and one set of weights reaching b. Follow through from the learner’s displayed work.
Identify the two zero y entries in the variant and obtain the final condition 0 = s − 4 or an equivalent equation. Accept a consistent equivalent elimination path.
For the consistent case, explain the planes’ common line and why equal columns allow infinitely many weights that reach b.
Give two distinct triples satisfying the consistent system. Accept any valid pair.

For the inconsistent case, explain why the third plane misses the common line, and why the first two right-hand-side coordinates force x + y = 3 and z = 1, so the third coordinate of the weighted sum is 4.
